turns: Which hubs in the Midwest are most exposed to winter disruption?
results.answer: Minneapolis (MSP) is the most exposed Midwest hub to winter disruption, with a winter score of 48.2. That is moderate, not high. Chicago (CHI, 39.9) and Detroit (DTW, 37.4) follow, and both are moderate. Kansas City (MCI) scores 33.8, just above the moderate threshold. Indianapolis (IND, 30.7) and Columbus (CMH, 30.1) are low. MSP is driven by 146.4 freeze days/yr (min temp <= 0 C) and 20.4 days/yr with snowfall >= 1 cm. CHI has 103.6 freeze days and 18.6 snow days >= 1 cm per year. CHI and DTW are not a close call, but CHI and MCI aren't either. The order of CHI vs DTW is a separate matter: CHI is a close call with the next hub, so its order against DTW is not meaningful.

turns: Compare Miami and Houston in terms of hurricane and flood exposure.
results.answer: Miami has the higher hurricane/wind exposure, and Houston has far higher flood exposure. On wind, Miami scores 51.9 (moderate) and Houston 43.1 (moderate). Miami has 11 FEMA wind declarations over 20 years against Houston's 8, and 11.8 days/yr with gusts of 60 km/h or more against 10.8. On flood, Houston scores 74.7 (high) and Miami 32.4 (low). Houston has 23.6 days/yr with 25 mm or more of rain, 4.2 days/yr with 50 mm or more, and 7 FEMA flood declarations. Miami has 9.2, 2.2 and 2 for the same measures. Overall, Houston's composite is 39.0 and Miami's is 22.7, both moderate or lower. Houston is the stronger candidate for flood resilience investment.

turns: What percentage of days in Denver last year had snowfall?
results.answer: In 2025, Denver had measurable snowfall (at least 0.1 cm) on 37 of 365 days, which is 10.1% of days. Snowfall of at least 1 cm occurred on 17 days, or 4.7%.

turns: Why is the Dallas hub's weather disruption risk high?
results.answer: Dallas's composite Weather Disruption Risk Score is 36.5, which is moderate, not high. The cut-off for high is 66. It ranks 2nd of 14 in the network, so it is relatively exposed even though its absolute score is moderate. Flood and heavy rain is the biggest driver. It adds 16.3 composite points. The flood score is 54.3, based on 16.2 days/yr with at least 25 mm of rain and 3.6 days/yr with at least 50 mm. Heat adds 6.8 points, from 54.6 days/yr above 35 C. Wind adds 9.9 points, partly from 5 FEMA wind declarations over 20 years. Winter is low and adds only 3.5 points.

results.answer: Chicago (CHI) ranks 2nd of 6 Midwest hubs for flood exposure. Its flood score is 30.8, which is low (below 33), so it is second only in relative terms. The main driver is FEMA flood, severe-storm and coastal-storm declarations (7 in 20 years, 18.7 points). Rain adds less: 5.8 days/yr with at least 25 mm and 0.4 days/yr with at least 50 mm. Kansas City is well ahead at 44.6. Minneapolis (29.8) is within 3 points of Chicago, so their order isn't meaningful. For the overall picture, Chicago's composite score is 25.9 (low), 7th of 14 in the network. Winter is its largest composite contributor at 12.0 points, then flood at 9.2.

turns: Which three hubs have the highest overall weather disruption risk?
results.answer: The top three hubs by composite Weather Disruption Risk Score are Houston (HOU, 39.0), Dallas (DFW, 36.5) and Newark (EWR, 33.4). All three score "moderate" (33 to 66), so they rank highest in the network but none is "high" in absolute terms. Houston's drivers are 23.6 days/yr with at least 25 mm of rain and 8 FEMA wind-type declarations over 20 years. Dallas's drivers are 16.2 rain days/yr at 25 mm or more and 54.6 days/yr above 35 C. Newark's drivers are 7 FEMA wind-type declarations over 20 years and 12.2 rain days/yr at 25 mm or more. Houston and Dallas are 2.5 points apart, so that order is reliable. Houston is flagged as a close call with Dallas, and Newark is flagged as a close call with the next hub, so their order against those neighbors is not meaningful.

turns: Which hubs face the biggest hurricane risk?
results.answer: Miami has the highest hurricane/wind score in the network at 51.9, followed by Newark at 43.3, Houston at 43.1 and Dallas at 39.6. Miami ranks first mainly because of 11 FEMA hurricane, tropical storm, tornado and wind declarations in 20 years, plus 11.8 days/yr with gusts of 60 km/h or more. Newark and Houston are a close call, so their order is not meaningful. Newark's score comes from 7 declarations and 20.4 gust days/yr. Houston's comes from 8 declarations and 10.8 gust days/yr. Atlanta is fifth at 26.6, which is low.

turns: Where is extreme heat the biggest problem for us?
results.answer: Phoenix (PHX) is the clear heat hotspot. Its heat score is 100 out of 100, which is high, driven by 137.4 days/yr with a max temperature of 35 C or more. Dallas (DFW) is a distant second at 45.5 (moderate), with 54.6 days/yr above 35 C. Houston (22.3, 26.8 days/yr), Denver (14.8, 17.8 days/yr) and Kansas City (10.0, 12.0 days/yr) are all low. Only Phoenix is high in absolute terms. Dallas ranks second but is only moderate.

turns: Why is Miami only moderate? It gets hurricanes all the time.
results.answer: Miami's hurricane and wind score is moderate (51.9). It is also the highest in the network for wind, ahead of Newark (43.3) and Houston (43.1). The premise needs one correction. Miami's composite score is 22.7, which is low, and it ranks 9th of 14. It is not moderate. Wind is the only hazard where Miami scores high relative to the other hubs. The composite blends four hazards: winter 30%, flood 30%, wind 25% and heat 15%. Miami scores 0.0 on winter and 0.2 on heat, so only wind (13.0 points) and flood (9.7 points) add to its composite. Wind itself is held below 'high' because FEMA declarations are the only wind indicator at its maximum: 11 declarations in 20 years, which maxes out that indicator and contributes 40 points. The measured wind days are modest. Gusts of 60 km/h or more occur 11.8 days/yr (8.8 points), and gusts of 90 km/h or more occur 0.2 days/yr (3.0 points). Flood is low at 32.4: 9.2 days/yr with 25 mm or more of rain, 2.2 days/yr with 50 mm or more, and 2 FEMA flood declarations.
